content: Viral warts are a prevalent dermatological condition that can vary in severity, ranging from minor, self-resolving lesions to persistent, chronic cases. Numerous topical treatments are available for managing these lesions. The objective of this study was to assess the efficacy of various topical treatments for non-genital cutaneous warts in healthy, immunocompetent adults and children. The analysis included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and was based on a comprehensive search of multiple databases up to May 2011. A total of 85 trials involving 8,815 participants were included in the review, with 26 new studies added in the latest update. The studies evaluated a wide range of treatments and employed diverse trial designs. Many of these studies were found to have a high risk of bias in one or more aspects of their methodology. Salicylic acid (SA) was shown to significantly improve wart clearance compared to placebo across all sites (risk ratio [RR] 1.56, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.20 to 2.03). Subgroup analyses suggested that SA might be more effective for warts on the hands (RR 2.67, 95% CI 1.43 to 5.01) than on the feet (RR 1.29, 95% CI 1.07 to 1.55). Cryotherapy, when compared to placebo, did not demonstrate a significant overall benefit (RR 1.45, 95% CI 0.65 to 3.23). Subgroup analyses suggested that cryotherapy might be more effective for hand warts (RR 2.63, 95% CI 0.43 to 15.94) than for foot warts (RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.26 to 3.07). One trial indicated that cryotherapy was superior to both placebo and SA, but only for warts on the hands. No significant differences in cure rates were observed between cryotherapy administered at 2-, 3-, or 4-week intervals. However, aggressive cryotherapy appeared more effective than gentle cryotherapy (RR 1.90, 95% CI 1.15 to 3.15), albeit with a higher incidence of adverse effects. A meta-analysis comparing cryotherapy and SA did not reveal a significant difference in effectiveness across all sites (RR 1.23, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.71) or in subgroup analyses for hands and feet. However, two trials involving 328 participants suggested that combining SA with cryotherapy was more effective than using SA alone (RR 1.24, 95% CI 1.07 to 1.43). The efficacy of intralesional bleomycin remains uncertain due to inconsistent evidence. The most informative trial, involving 31 participants, found no significant difference in cure rates between bleomycin and saline injections (RR 1.28, 95% CI 0.92 to 1.78). Dinitrochlorobenzene was found to be more than twice as effective as placebo in two trials involving 80 participants (RR 2.12, 95% CI 1.38 to 3.26). Conversely, two trials of clear duct tape with 193 participants showed no significant advantage over placebo (RR 1.43, 95% CI 0.51 to 4.05). Data from trials evaluating other treatments, such as intralesional 5-fluorouracil, topical zinc, silver nitrate, topical 5-fluorouracil, pulsed dye laser, photodynamic therapy, 80% phenol, 5% imiquimod cream, intralesional antigen, and topical alpha-lactalbumin-oleic acid, could not be pooled. Some of these treatments, such as silver nitrate, showed potential benefits, while others, like topical alpha-lactalbumin-oleic acid, demonstrated no advantage over placebo. No RCTs were identified for surgical interventions (e.g., curettage, excision) or for treatments such as formaldehyde, podophyllotoxin, cantharidin, diphencyprone, or squaric acid dibutylester. In conclusion, the evidence for the effectiveness of SA is more consistent, though its therapeutic effect is modest. Cryotherapy did not show a significant advantage over placebo or SA in most trials, except for one study that demonstrated its superiority for hand warts. Adverse effects, including pain, blistering, and scarring, were more commonly associated with cryotherapy, though these were not consistently reported. Other treatments reviewed did not appear to be safer or more effective than SA or cryotherapy. Clear duct tape showed no benefit over placebo, while dinitrochlorobenzene and similar contact sensitizers may be useful for refractory warts.
